title: RL-ATTACK: A Generalized Black-Box Adversarial Attack on Language Models via Reinforcement Learning

Title:RL-ATTACK: A Generalized Black-Box Adversarial Attack on Language Models via Reinforcement Learning
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Large language models (LLMs) exhibit vulnerabilities to adversarial perturbations that can induce unintended responses. These vulnerabilities can be identified via intentional attacks and subsequently used to improve model safety. In black-box settings where gradients are inaccessible, existing methods tend to guess adversarial transformations using external knowledge, ignoring the information provided by the target model. To mitigate this, we propose a trainable black-box framework based on reinforcement learning, which learns from the target model to generate tailored adversarial transformations. We demonstrate that our approach achieves lower post-attack accuracy, greater query efficiency and better semantic preservation on both natural language inference and generative Q&A tasks. On natural language inference, it drives post-attack accuracy to 2% within 20 queries. Against generative language models, our trained attacker consistently achieves lower post-attack accuracy than the untrained attacker and wins in 4 out of 6 settings when compared to a strong optimization-based baseline. We further experiment with multiple reward designs and training settings, and we find that no design or setting is consistently dominant. Our code is available at this https URL.

report.summary: RL-ATTACK trains a reinforcement-learning black-box attacker to generate adversarial transformations for language models, improving query efficiency and reducing post-attack accuracy.
report.background: Large language models are vulnerable to adversarial perturbations—small input changes that can produce unintended or unsafe outputs. Identifying these weaknesses through controlled attacks is a core part of safety evaluation and red-teaming. In black-box settings, attackers cannot access model gradients and must rely on queries. The paper argues that many existing black-box methods use external knowledge or handcrafted transformations to guess useful perturbations, rather than learning from the target model’s responses. This can waste queries and produce unnatural text. RL-ATTACK addresses this by framing attack generation as a trainable reinforcement-learning problem: an attacker policy learns from feedback from the target model to produce tailored transformations. The authors evaluate the approach on natural language inference and generative question answering, comparing it with untrained attackers and optimization-based baselines. The work sits at the intersection of LLM safety, adversarial robustness, and automated red-teaming, where query efficiency and semantic preservation are important because realistic attackers operate under limited access and detection pressure.
key_points: RL-ATTACK treats the attacker as a trainable reinforcement-learning policy rather than a fixed set of rules. It learns from the target model’s query responses to generate adversarial transformations tailored to that model, which is important in black-box settings where gradients are unavailable and external knowledge may be misleading.

On natural language inference, the method drives post-attack accuracy down to 2% within 20 queries. The authors also report greater query efficiency and better semantic preservation than prior approaches, meaning attacks need fewer model calls and produce text that remains closer to the original meaning.

Against generative language models, the trained attacker consistently outperforms an untrained attacker and wins four of six settings against a strong optimization-based baseline. This suggests learned black-box attackers can compete with optimization methods while using target-model feedback more directly.

The paper tests multiple reward designs and training settings and finds no single configuration is consistently dominant. That caveat matters for reproducibility and deployment: attack effectiveness depends on how rewards are shaped, so defenders and researchers should evaluate across settings rather than assume one universal recipe.

The authors release code, which lowers the barrier for red-teamers and researchers to reproduce the attacks and test defenses. It also raises dual-use concerns, since query-efficient attack tools can be misused if released without safeguards or usage guidance.
report.impact: RL-ATTACK shifts black-box LLM red-teaming toward adaptive, learned attackers that improve with target feedback. For the AI industry, it reinforces that safety evaluations should include query-efficient black-box attacks, not just gradient-based or handcrafted probes. Model providers may need stronger query monitoring, rate limiting, anomaly detection, and adversarial training. For developers, the work offers a template for stress-testing deployed models and agent pipelines, but also a reminder that attack code is dual-use and should be handled in controlled environments. For regular users, the near-term effect is indirect: better robustness testing could improve model safety, but the same techniques could enable more targeted manipulation if abused. The paper’s mixed reward-design findings also caution against treating any single attack or defense as definitive.
report.tools: To follow up, start with the paper’s released code, then compare it with established NLP attack libraries such as TextAttack and OpenAttack. The Adversarial Robustness Toolbox (ART) is useful for broader threat modeling, Hugging Face Transformers for target models and evaluation, and Stable-Baselines3 or TRL for reinforcement-learning attacker training. Use these only in controlled red-team environments with clear authorization and logging.
